title: Ask with a brief, not a compliment
summary: Replace impressive-sounding role prompts with four lines you can check.
outcome: Write a four-line brief that another person could evaluate without guessing.

sections.title: Why “act like an expert” adds nothing
sections.body:
A role instruction changes tone, not access. It does not give the model your policy, your data or your standard. If the task fails, a role prompt gives you nothing to repair.

A brief gives you four things you can check: the task, the source, the audience and the shape of the output.

sections.title: The four-line brief
sections.body:
```text
Task: Turn the eight messages below into a triage table.
Source: Use only the messages in this chat. Do not add outside facts.
Audience: A shift supervisor who has 30 seconds.
Output: A table with id, category, urgency and reason. Then three bullets of what needs a human.
Rule: If a message is unclear, write NEEDS REVIEW instead of guessing.
```

The last line matters most. It tells the model what to do when the input is incomplete, which is where confident invention usually starts.

sections.title: Test it before you trust it
sections.body:
Run the brief on one easy case and one deliberately incomplete case. If the incomplete case produces a confident category, the rule failed.

Repair the brief, not the answer. A prompt that needs three corrections after every run is not a prompt, it is a conversation you keep repeating.

checks: My brief names a task, a source, an audience and an output shape.
It says what to do when information is missing.
I tested it on an incomplete input.
